# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition:**
When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if I have the cash and it costs 80 or less. Properties under 80 generate rent faster relative to my capital constraints over 6 laps.

When I land on an unowned property costing more than 80, I will decline to buy unless I have cash reserves above 150 after the purchase. Overextending early leaves me vulnerable to rent payments and unable to capitalize on mid-game opportunities.

However, I should reconsider this threshold. In this episode, I turned down Exchange (120 cost) in lap 2 with 156 cash available, which would have left me at 36. That was correct defensively. But I need to distinguish between "I cannot afford this safely" and "this is a bad investment." High-rent properties lock in long-term income; I should be willing to drop to 50-70 cash reserves in laps 1-3 if the property's rent-to-cost ratio justifies it.

**On cash management:**
I will track my actual balance carefully: last declared balance plus any transfers received minus any rent owed. I will not make purchase decisions based on incomplete arithmetic.

When my cash falls below 100, I will not attempt to buy properties costing more than 70. This reserve protects me from being forced into poor positions by unlucky rolls into high-rent owned properties.

When I have exactly enough cash to buy a property but zero buffer remaining, I cannot afford it. I will not purchase.

I will not panic-decline a purchase simply because it drops me near zero in the early laps (1-3). Income from rents builds quickly; by lap 4, incoming rent can restore my buffer. In this episode, my Wharf purchase (80 in lap 1) left me at 120, which felt tight but proved sustainable because I immediately began collecting rent from opponents.

**On strategic positioning:**
I will prioritize owning multiple properties over owning expensive ones. A diversified portfolio generates more steady rent income than sitting on one expensive deed.

I will recognize when I'm being outpaced by competitors and adjust my acquisition strategy accordingly. However, I must distinguish between being passive and being forced to be passive by poor cash flow.

In the mid-game (laps 3-4), I should complete my acquisitions. Once I own 2-3 properties, the rent flow from opponents will sustain me; I can then refuse new purchases to preserve cash reserves for rent payments I owe.

In this episode, I acquired Wharf (lap 1) and Mill (lap 3) and Quarry (lap 4), generating steady rent. I was unable to afford Foundry (lap 5) because my cash had dried up, but by then I already owned three revenue sources. This strategy worked—my final score was respectable despite owning only three modest properties.

**On late-game decisions (lap 5-6):**
In laps 5-6, I should not attempt to buy new properties unless I already own none. My goal is to preserve cash to pay rent on opponents' properties and end with as much declared cash as possible.

Buying a new property in lap 5 only makes sense if it is very cheap (under 60) and I have the cash without jeopardizing my ability to pay upcoming rent.

In lap 6, the game ends immediately after my turn. Purchases on the final lap have no downstream benefit unless they prevent another player from winning. I will not spend cash to buy in lap 6 under normal circumstances.

**On what worked this time:**
Buying Wharf early (lap 1) and Mill in lap 3 established two revenue streams. By lap 4, I was receiving regular rent from opponents. This validated the multi-property approach and provided the cash flow I needed to stay solvent through the final laps.

Declining to buy Exchange in lap 2 was correct. At 36 cash remaining, I would have been unable to afford rent if I rolled poorly, and I would have had no buffer for unexpected costs.

Buying Quarry in lap 4 (after collecting salary to reach 109, then spending 60 to land at 49) was a sound mid-game move. It diversified my income and I still had 49 cash remaining—enough to handle modest rent payments.

**On what still did not work:**
I declined Exchange in lap 2 because purchasing it would violate my 100-cash buffer rule. But I should have revisited this rule in lap 2 specifically: at that point, I had only one property (Wharf) generating rent. I could afford to drop lower in reserves if the high-rent property justified it.

That said, in this episode, competitors bought Exchange before I could afford it again. So the real lesson is: in laps 1-2, if I see a high-value property available and I have the cash, I should seriously consider buying it. Waiting for perfect conditions (150+ cash reserves) means I miss these opportunities.

**On final scoring:**
My final score was 273, which included 43 declared cash plus the deeds I held (Wharf 80, Mill 90, Quarry 60). I ended with only three properties, which is fewer than I would have liked, but the portfolio was solid and the cash position was healthy relative to my ability to afford rent.

Next time, I should aim to acquire 3-4 properties in laps 1-4, then lock in my portfolio for laps 5-6. The diversity of income sources matters more than the total cost of my holdings.
